extracted.intended_audience: journalists and journalism students (also educators and others who use the Five Ws)
extracted.subtask_short: writing news leads with Five Ws
extracted.subtask_description: Using the Five Ws checklist (Who, What, Where, When, Why — and often How) to ensure a news lead or report contains the essential factual points; also guidance for using the questions in research and interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who?
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Five Ws: 'Who?'. Reporters are taught the lead should answer who is involved in the situation being reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the person(s) or actors responsible or affected. Use 'Who?' in the lead and in reporting to make clear who the story is about; use it when guiding research and interviews to elicit the responsible parties or subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: What?
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Five Ws: 'What?'. The lead should state what happened — the facts or event at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize the central event, action, or fact of the story. 'What?' should convey the core occurrence so readers understand the story's substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where?
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Five Ws: 'Where?'. The lead should say where the event occurred or the location context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify location or setting relevant to the story. Use geographic detail appropriate to the audience and the significance of place.

rubrics_metrics.name: When?
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Five Ws: 'When?'. The lead should indicate the timing of the event or action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide date/time or temporal context so readers understand recency, sequence, or urgency. Timing can affect news value and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why?
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Five Ws: 'Why?'. The lead (or subsequent reporting) should address reasons, motives, or causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain purpose, motive, or cause where possible. The page highlights Aristotle's view that 'Why' is especially important for understanding actions; use it to provide explanation rather than mere description.

rubrics_metrics.name: How? (the H)
rubrics_metrics.description: The optional sixth interrogative often paired with the Five Ws: 'How?' or 'In what way?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe manner, method, or means by which something happened. The page notes 'the Five Ws (and How)' and that many formulations include this H; include it when method/means are important to understanding the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Five Ws as a checklist for the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The Five Ws is a checklist used in journalism to ensure that the lead contains all the essential points of a story: Who, What, Where, Why, When (and sometimes How).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As far back as 1913 reporters were taught that the lead should answer these questions. Use the Five Ws to structure leads so essential information is conveyed up front; they also serve as an organizing device for initial reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Five Ws to guide research, interviews, and ethical scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters use the Five Ws to guide research and interviews and to raise important ethical questions (for example, 'How do you know that?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Ws as prompts in interviews and source evaluation to probe evidence, attribution, and reliability. They are tools for both information-gathering and for checking claims and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/expanded 'elements of circumstances' (Septem Circumstantiae)
rubrics_metrics.description: A classical rhetorical/legal formulation of circumstances (used by Aristotle, Hermagoras, Cicero, Aquinas etc.) that maps onto and sometimes expands the Ws: who, what, where, when, why, how, with what (quibus auxiliis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The seven elements were used to particularize, explain, or predict circumstances of action; historical guidance includes questions about instruments/means ('with what') and modality. The page notes their use in rhetoric, moral evaluation, and law (e.g., distinguishing voluntary from involuntary action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern practice caveat: not always cram all Ws into first sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: By the 1940s the practice of answering all Five Ws in the first sentence (the traditional lead) was criticized as old-fashioned; many stories now use more supple feature leads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigidly forcing every W into the opening sentence if it harms readability or narrative flow; consider feature/interpretive leads that unfold details while still ensuring essential facts are covered somewhere early in the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in data analytics (BADIR) to identify problem and context
rubrics_metrics.description: In data analytics the Five Ws are used in the first stage of the BADIR process to identify the business problem and its context in an analytics request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Ws to clarify the business question: who is affected, what outcome is desired, where/when the problem occurs, why it matters, and how results will be used. This frames analytic scope and requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in military five paragraph order to convey tactical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Militaries use the Five Ws to convey the details of tactical tasks within a broader mission as part of the five paragraph order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Ws to transmit concise tasking: who will do what, where, when, why (purpose), and how (method), ensuring clarity of orders and responsibilities.
